text.content:
Woolly Bay (Days 30–36)

GM page, with three read-alouds. Days 30 to 36, up Woolly Bay from the Highport reach. The second read-aloud plants @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GBckJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GbPgSetup00]{the Grey-Back}: it has to happen, and the table has to be allowed to dismiss it.

Read aloud — the morning after

The morning of Day 30. Read the bracketed line that fits how the crew line went in the boarding.

Morning comes up grey and flat over a sea with nothing on it. The Grey Fee is gone, or a hulk astern on a long line, or a smudge on the horizon, and nobody aboard talks about her at all.

There is work instead. The rail is stove in where the irons came over, and the carpenter is at it with a saw before the dew is off. The deck is sanded, twice. The Grey Fee's dead went over the side last night with ballast at their feet and no words said, and nobody looks at the place.

[If any of the crew died:] Your own dead are sewn into their hammocks on the hatch cover, and at noon Master Roke reads the words over them himself, from a little book he has plainly read from before, and they go over the side together.

[If none of the crew died:] At noon Master Roke opens a cask of the good wine for the whole crew, which nobody aboard has ever seen him do, drinks one cup with them and goes below.

And from that morning on, the Kestrel Wife puts in at no more ports that nobody told you about.

Read aloud — a grey-back follows a bloody hull

Day 31, at the evening meal. Let the players hear it, watch Roke dismiss it, and dismiss it too.

It is the bosun who says it first, at the evening meal, to nobody in particular, with his eyes on his bowl: that a grey-back follows a bloody hull. That they put the Grey Fee's dead over the side two nights ago, and blood carries further in the water than you would think, and something has been keeping station astern of them ever since. He has seen it twice, he says. A fin like a sail, a long way off.

Two of the older hands nod. Wick Ferrin laughs, and then stops laughing when nobody joins in.

Master Roke does not look up from his plate. “Stow it,” he says, quite mildly. “There's no grey-backs this far up the bay, and if there were they'd want a whale, not a wool hull. Eat your supper.”

The bosun eats his supper. Afterwards, on deck, you see him at the stern rail, looking back along the wake for a long time.

Read aloud — up the bay

Days 32 to 36. About thirty seconds.

The days run together. The rail is patched, and then patched again where the first patch sprang. The wind comes round into the north and stays there, cold, and the Kestrel Wife beats up the bay against it in long slow tacks, a mile gained for every two sailed. On the thirty-fifth day a thin rain sets in, and does not stop.

The crew stop talking about grey-backs where Roke can hear them. They do not stop looking astern. Once, in the rain, the lookout sings out at something behind the ship, and by the time anybody reaches the rail there is nothing there but the wake.

GM notes

  • Count the dead from the boarding's crew line: none, one or two. Whoever died had a name the party knew. The burial is the only time the intermission asks the table to stand still, so let it.
  • Do not let anyone see the grey-back before Day 37. The point of the plant is that the table hears it and dismisses it with Roke; a sighting turns a consequence into a hunt.
  • Roke has changed. No more unannounced ports, no explanation, and more wine at his table than before. If anyone asks him directly, he gives the Highport line on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1NpcsJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1NpPgRoke000]{his page}.
  • Wick Ferrin is cheerful, talks about the midwinter baby, and is the one who laughs at the bosun. That is all he needs to be.

The Grey-Back

Scene: @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-scenes.Scene.BR2T1ScnSea00000]{Intermission 1 — The Kestrel Wife at Sea} — the same hull as the boarding, eight days on. GM pins mark the rudder (hull track) and the patched rail.

Day 37, inside Woolly Bay, the third day of thin rain. The rail is patched where the irons tore her, they are short whatever hands the boarding cost them, and something has been keeping station astern since the Pomarj.

Plant it on day 31

The crew have been saying it for a week and @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-actors.Actor.BR2T1ActRoke0000]{Master Orin Roke} has been telling them to stow it. A grey-back follows a bloody hull, and they put the Grey Fee's dead over the side in one evening. The scene is on @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1GBckJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1GbPgBay0000]{Woolly Bay (Days 30–36)}. Let the players hear the superstition, let them watch Roke dismiss it, and let them dismiss it too.

Read aloud

Day 37, just after the forenoon watch changes. About forty seconds; roll initiative on the last line.

The wheel goes heavy just after the forenoon watch changes.

Not fouled, not jammed — heavy, the way a door is heavy when somebody is leaning on the other side of it. The man at the helm braces a foot on the binnacle and hauls, and the ship answers him about half as much as she should, and then not at all, and then all at once.

Roke comes up from below without his coat. He looks over the stern for a long moment at nothing, at grey water going by, and says, in a perfectly ordinary voice: “Get the cod up on deck. All of it.”

Then the whole ship shudders, forward of the mainmast, from underneath.

The Pack — Enemies & Tactics

EnemyCountCRXP eachTotal
Giant shark — the grey-back151,8001,800
Hunter shark — the pack that has been feeding behind her324501,350
Encounter total3,150 XP

Six PCs: a fourth hunter shark (+450).

Both are SRD, so both are in whatever monster compendium you have. As with the ankhegs, use your compendium's numbers rather than any written here; what matters is the shape. The giant shark is the right monster for this table for one specific reason: low armour and a great many hit points. Four ranged chassis will land nearly everything they throw and still need three or four rounds, so the fight lasts long enough for the clocks to bite without ever threatening a wipe. Its blood frenzy is where the danger actually lives — advantage against anything already wounded, which means the people in the water, not the people on deck.

How it fights

It is not attacking the party. It is attacking the ship, because the ship is the wounded thing it has been following, and it does not distinguish between a hull and a whale. It rams at the end of any round in which nothing is bleeding in the water. The pack works the surface and takes anything that falls.

It has no interest in boarding, cannot reach the deck, and will not chase a target out of the water. Every hit point of threat it presents has to be delivered through the hull or through somebody who is swimming — which is why the encounter has three objectives and no kill requirement.

pages.name: Ship Damage, the Overboard Clock & the Bait

text.content:
Ship Damage, the Overboard Clock & the Bait

1. The hull — a four-segment track

Mark one segment each time the grey-back rams.

SegmentThe Kestrel Wife
1Steering goes heavy. DC 12 to hold a course; a failure means a round broadside to the swell and everyone on deck makes DC 10 or goes prone.
2The rudder head is sprung. She can only be steered with the sweeps — four hands occupied for the rest of the voyage.
3A plank starts. Two people on the pump from here to Hardby, in shifts, and one of them will be a PC.
4She is taking water faster than the pump. Hardby is three days off. Nobody drowns — she limps in, and the customs mole looks at her repairs rather than at her bales.

Segment 4 is not a fail state. It is a different arrival, and it touches @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3ArrivalJrnl.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3ArPgArr02Cmm]{Arrival — Commercial Cover}: the harbour that was written to take them in without a flicker now has a reason to ask one question. Let it.

2. Two in the water — two rounds each

The first strike takes a hand off the rail. Name him days ago. He is Wick Ferrin, he has a wife in Gradsul with their first child due at midwinter, and he taught Elle to splice on day nineteen. Two rounds to get him out before the pack has him; the grey-back's blood frenzy triggers off him the moment he is hurt.

Read aloud — man overboard

On the first strike, round one.

The ship heels as though she had struck a rock, and every loose thing on deck slides. Wick Ferrin, out on the rail with a line in his hands, goes over it without a sound.

For a moment there is only the hole in the water where he went in. Then his head comes up, twenty feet off the side, hair plastered flat, shouting something nobody can hear over the ship. And around him, in three places at once, the grey water begins to cut.

This is the choice the encounter is built on. A party that spends its first two rounds killing sharks loses him. A party that spends them on the rescue eats two more rams and arrives on segment 3 or 4. There is no clever third answer and you should not invent one.

3. The bait — the smart win

The hold has salt cod in it, and a crew who have already told them what grey-backs follow, and Roke shouts for the cod in his read-aloud because he has done this before. Anyone who puts it together — stave the barrels over the lee side, get the blood-water away from the hull — ends the fight: the pack goes at it, and the big one turns into the frenzy on the wrong side of the ship. Award the full XP. A table that solves a monster with cargo has done the thing the whole intermission is teaching them to do.

The grey-back also breaks off on its own at a third of its hit points if there is enough blood elsewhere in the water — so a party that wounds it badly and then chums gets the same result at a higher price.

Underwater Rules at the Table

Have these to hand before anybody jumps in, and say the first one out loud before Selvara picks a spell rather than after.

Fire. A fully submerged creature has resistance to fire damage. That is the rule as written and it is the one that will come up.

Ranged weapon attacks made underwater are at disadvantage inside normal range and automatically miss beyond it. From the tops, shooting at something on the surface, none of that applies — Gianni has clean shots all fight and should be told so.

Melee underwater is at disadvantage for a creature without a swim speed, unless the weapon is a dagger, javelin, shortsword, spear or trident. A monk's unarmed strikes are not on that list.

Do not invent a lightning-in-water bonus. There isn't one, and a ruling made here to be generous becomes an argument in Phase 8 when somebody wants it in a flooded gallery.

Who this encounter belongs to

Kitty. She is the only person aboard who can meet it in its own element, and a druid who spends a wild shape to go into black water after a drowning sailor is doing the bravest thing in the intermission. Build the beat for her; let the others hold the deck.

Alicia's eldritch blast is force damage and cares about none of the rules above, and a repelling blast will shove three hundred pounds of shark off a rudder. Let that work exactly as she hopes. Elle should get one moment out along the sweep or the stern rail with nothing under her. Selvara is the one the rules bite, and the fair thing is to tell her before she spends the slot.

Outcomes

Read aloud — when it ends

When the fight ends. Read the lines that fit, then the close.

[If they killed it:] It comes up alongside on its back, white belly to the rain, twenty feet of it, and rolls once, and lies still. Nobody cheers. Then everybody does.

[If they drove it off, or baited it:] Out on the lee side the water boils pink over the salt cod, and the great grey shape turns into the frenzy with the rest of them and goes down, and does not come back up. The sea goes flat and grey and empty, as if nothing had ever happened in it.

[If Wick Ferrin was lost:] Where he was, there is only the rain on the water. Nobody says his name. Somebody coils the line he was holding when he went, very neatly, and hangs it on its pin.

[If the hull reached segment 3 or 4:] Below, the pump starts its clanking, and does not stop.

Then the rain comes on harder, and Master Roke takes the helm himself.

Killed it. Twenty feet of grey-back alongside and a crew who will not stop talking about it. The jaw comes aboard. It is worth nothing and they will never part with it, and it hangs in the Kestrel Wife's waist for the rest of the campaign, and if the party ever sees that ship again it is the first thing they recognise.

Drove it off or baited it. The better ending, honestly. Nobody won; the sea lost interest. Roke's opinion of them goes up more for this than for killing it.

Lost Ferrin. Do not soften it and do not punish them with it. He goes under, the water closes, and the fight carries on for two more rounds because it has to. What it costs is the crew's warmth for the last three days, and that silence is worth more at the rail on day forty than any mechanical consequence.

Hull at segment 4. They arrive pumping. See the hand-off page for the two lines of the canon arrival read-aloud that want adjusting.

The Last of the Bay (Days 38–40)

GM page, with two read-alouds and the hand-off. The party should have made 6th level at the rail on Day 37 (@UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1QRefJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1QrPgXP00000]{XP and the Sixth-Level Line}). If they have not, award it here, on the deck, and not on the Hardby quay.

Read aloud — the last of the bay

Days 38 and 39. Read the bracketed line that fits the hull track.

The rain stops. The bay narrows. On the western shore a town goes by in the haze, walls and smoke and a crowded harbour — Fax, the crew say — and nobody suggests putting in.

[If the hull reached segment 3 or 4:] Two at a time, day and night, there is somebody on the pump, and the clank of it becomes the sound the ship makes, like a heartbeat. Everybody takes a turn. Nobody complains, and nobody talks much either.

[Otherwise:] The Kestrel Wife runs north with the wind behind her for the first time in a week, and the crew sing at the pumps again — the filthy one.

On the last night, Master Roke comes and stands beside you at the rail for a long time without saying anything at all.

Then, to whichever of them is awake.

[If any of the crew died on the voyage:] “I'll not ask,” he says at last. “But when you're ashore, and you're doing whatever it is — there were eleven of us on this hull out of Gradsul, and there aren't now. I'd like it to have been for something.”

[If nobody died:] “I'll not ask,” he says at last, and goes back to his charts.

Day 40 — Hardby, at dusk

Read @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.phase-3-journals.JournalEntry.BR2P3ArrivalJrnl.JournalEntryPage.BR2P3ArPgArr02Cmm]{Arrival — Commercial Cover}, with the two lines @UUID[Compendium.blooming-rot-2.travel-1-journals.JournalEntry.BR2T1QRefJrnl000.JournalEntryPage.BR2T1QrPgHandoff]{Hand-off to Phase 3} adjusts; they are written out there, ready to read. Before you do, put four things on the back of the hand-off sheet: the visibility tier, the hull track, the crew's dead, and the Gull's papers (docket y/n, weigh-ticket y/n).

And if the grey-back's jaw came aboard, it is hanging in the Kestrel Wife's waist as she ties up. It stays there for the rest of the campaign.
